analysis.one_liner: Lets bank, brokerage, and insurance customers block their financial institutions from sharing or selling their account information.
analysis.headline: The Senate Banking Committee held one hearing on the bill in June 1999 and never voted on it; it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill told federal banking regulators and the Securities and Exchange Commission to write rules giving customers of banks, brokerages, and insurers control over their personal financial data. A customer could send a written notice blocking sharing even with a company's own affiliates, and the company would need the customer's explicit consent before passing account information to outside businesses. Institutions would have to explain exactly what data could go where, let customers check their records for errors, and answer to a complaint process. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, got a single hearing, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Customers of banks, savings institutions, brokerages, and insurance companies: anyone with a deposit account, certificate of deposit, securities holding, or insurance policy would gain notice and the right to stop or approve sharing of their transaction records, balances, and payouts.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a financial institution from sharing confidential customer data with its own affiliates or agents once the customer sends a written notice forbidding it, with notice given when the relationship starts and at least once a year after.
Prohibits sharing confidential customer information with any outside company unless the customer has given informed written or electronic consent first.
Requires institutions to tell customers specifically what information could be shared, with what kinds of businesses, and for what purposes — not just a vague blanket notice.
Gives customers access to the data that could be shared so they can review it for accuracy and correct or supplement it, and sets up an enforcement and consumer complaint process.

Preserves necessary exceptions: information can still flow for processing a transaction the customer authorized, to regulators, to courts, and to credit bureaus for purposes already allowed under the Fair Credit Reporting Act.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, savings institutions, securities firms, and insurers bear the compliance costs of notices, consent handling, record access, and examinations, and they lose revenue from sharing or selling customer account data with affiliates and marketing partners.

drawbacks.text: The affiliate rule is opt-out, not opt-in: sharing inside a corporate family continues by default unless the customer affirmatively sends a written notice, so many customers who never respond would still have data flowing among affiliates.

The bill carves out credit reporting agencies — a bank can still pass customer information to a credit bureau, which can then appear in consumer reports released to third parties for permissible purposes.

Compliance would impose real costs on thousands of institutions of all sizes — separate notices, consent tracking, record-access systems, and examinations — costs that smaller community banks argued would fall hardest on them, though the bill text itself does not scale the requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections are broad and the compliance burden is the kind that any functioning notice-and-consent system carries; the honest objection is that the opt-out default for affiliates leaves a large amount of sharing untouched unless customers act, and the credit-bureau carve-out keeps a significant channel open. On balance the bill gives customers substantially more control than the status quo, and the costs fall on the institutions that profit from the data.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee took the bill up only far enough to hold one hearing, then never wrote or voted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Sarbanes introduced the bill on January 19, 1999, joined by Senators Dodd, Bryan, Leahy, Edwards, and Hollings; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee.
The bill drew 7 cosponsors, 6 of them Democrats and 1 a Republican.
The Committee on Banking held hearings on the bill on June 9, 1999 — the only substantive action it ever received.
No markup was ever scheduled and the bill was never reported out of committee; it died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial institutions came out ahead: banks, brokerages, and insurers kept the ability to share and sell customers' account information without their consent, and the stronger privacy rules this bill would have mandated never existed. Late in the same Congress, Congress did enact financial-modernization legislation that rewrote financial-services law, but the privacy protections it contained were weaker than what this bill proposed (widely reported).

for.name: Paul Sarbanes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 7 Senate cosponsors (6 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senators Dodd, Bryan, Leahy, Edwards, and Hollings.

for.name: Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill on June 9, 1999.

against.name: Phil Gramm
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in his committee after the June 1999 hearing; he never scheduled a markup or brought it to a vote before the Congress ended. During this period the committee's legislative effort went to the financial-modernization bill that became law instead.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but tilted Democratic — the sponsor and 6 of 7 cosponsors were Democrats, with 1 Republican — and because the bill never got a vote, no one ever had to go on record for or against it.

industries.note: The bill would bar them from sharing deposit-account, certificate-of-deposit, and transaction data with affiliates without a customer opt-out and with outside companies without consent, cutting off a revenue stream from customer information. Because the bill died, they kept that data-sharing business intact.
As institutions under SEC jurisdiction, they would face the same consent and notice rules for customers' securities holdings. The bill's death left their use of account data unrestricted.

Insurance policy records were covered as confidential customer information, so insurers would have needed customer consent before sharing policy and payout data. The bill's death preserved their data-sharing practices.
The bill expressly allowed banks to keep passing customer information to credit bureaus for Fair Credit Reporting Act purposes, locking in their access to bank data even under the proposed rules.
